title: Storing, handling & stock control of materials
blurb: Stock rotation, expiry dates, reorder levels, the medicines fridge, prescription-only medicine deliveries and COSHH storage.
question: A delivery arrives containing local anaesthetic cartridges, a box of composite and a glucagon kit. The fridge thermometer reads 11 °C and nobody has filled in the temperature log for three days. What do you do with each item, and what must happen about the fridge?

teach.h: Why stock control is a clinical skill
teach.body: Materials and medicines only work as intended if they are in date and have been stored correctly. Composite left in sunlight, alginate that has absorbed moisture, or a drug kept too warm may fail without looking any different. Good stock control means the right items are always available, nothing is used past its expiry date, nothing is wasted through over-ordering, and hazardous substances are stored safely. It is also about managing the practice's time and money well.

steps.label: Check against the order
steps.sub: Delivery note matches what was ordered

steps.label: POMs secured
steps.sub: Checked and locked away by an authorised person

steps.label: Record and rotate
steps.sub: Update stock records; new stock behind old

teach.caption: POM = prescription-only medicine, such as local anaesthetic cartridges.

teach.h: Stock rotation: first in, first out (FIFO)
teach.caption: Put new stock behind older stock so the item that expires soonest is used first. Check expiry dates when you stock up and before every use.

teach.body: Each item has a minimum (reorder) level: when stock falls to it, you order more, so you never run out mid-list. A maximum level stops over-ordering, which wastes money and space and leaves stock expiring on the shelf. If a critical item is running low, order more (or ask whoever orders) and tell the person who manages stock. Regular stock-takes keep the records accurate. Expired medicines are not used; they go in the blue-lidded medicinal waste bin.

teach.caption: Record the current, minimum and maximum temperature every working day, then reset the thermometer. The fridge is for medicines only: no food or drink.

items.label: glucagon shelf life if kept out of the fridge (below 25 °C)
emergency drugs and equipment check (at least)

teach.caption: If glucagon is moved out of the fridge, write the new, shorter expiry date on the box.

teach.h: COSHH hazards you'll find in the stock room

rows.label: Glucagon kit, some materials (check the label)

teach.note: Always follow the manufacturer's storage instructions and the safety data sheet (SDS).

teach.body: Under COSHH, every hazardous substance has a risk assessment and a safety data sheet kept where staff can find them. Store chemicals in their original labelled containers with lids on, never decanted into unmarked bottles. Keep incompatible substances apart: hypochlorite must not be stored with acids, because together they release chlorine gas. Store flammables away from heat and ignition sources, keep heavy and corrosive items low down, and make sure spill kits, including a mercury spill kit, are available.

teach.text: If the fridge has gone out of 2–8 °C, don't just turn the dial and carry on. Quarantine the contents (label 'do not use'), report it to the person responsible, record what happened and get advice from the manufacturer or a pharmacist before anything is used.

items: Check deliveries against the order; POMs are checked and locked away by an authorised person.
Rotate stock (FIFO): new stock goes behind old; check expiry dates before use.
Medicines fridge 2–8 °C, recorded daily; out-of-range stock is quarantined and reported.
Use reorder levels; tell the stock manager when a critical item runs low.
COSHH: original labelled containers, SDS available, incompatibles apart, spill kits ready.

summary: You can now receive and check a delivery, store POMs securely, rotate stock by FIFO and check expiry dates, keep and act on fridge temperature records, use reorder levels sensibly, and store hazardous substances safely under COSHH.

A.q: Why does the practice record the medicines fridge temperature every day?
options: To work out how much the fridge costs to run
Because the fridge has to be defrosted each day
To prove staff food is being kept separately
So temperature-sensitive items stay effective
A.why: Some drugs and materials lose effectiveness if they get too warm or freeze. Daily records show they have stayed within 2–8 °C.

whyNot.0: Running costs aren't the reason for temperature monitoring.
whyNot.1: Fridges don't need daily defrosting; the record is about the contents.
whyNot.2: Staff food shouldn't be in a medicines fridge at all.

A.q: A new box of composite arrives. Where should you put it on the shelf?
options: Behind the older boxes
In front of the older boxes
On top of the older boxes
In a separate cupboard
A.why: Stock rotation (first in, first out) means the older stock, which expires first, is at the front and used first.

whyNot.1: New stock at the front means older stock is left to expire.
whyNot.2: Stacking on top still makes the newest box the one picked first.
whyNot.3: Separating stock makes it easy to forget the older boxes.

A.q: You are asked to sign for a delivery of prescription-only medicines. What is the main consideration?
options: Sign quickly so the courier isn't kept waiting
Leave the box in reception until a dentist is free
Check it, then an authorised person locks it away
Open the boxes and count every cartridge before signing
A.why: POM deliveries must be checked against the order and stored securely by an authorised person, so medicines can't go missing or be misused.

whyNot.0: Signing without checking means errors or missing items go unnoticed.
whyNot.1: Leaving medicines unattended in reception is a security risk.
whyNot.3: Checking against the order matters, but the key point is secure storage by an authorised person.

B.q: What temperature range should the medicines fridge be kept within?
B.why: Medicines that need refrigeration are stored between 2 and 8 °C.

whyNot.0: Close to 0 °C risks freezing, which can damage medicines.
whyNot.3: 8–15 °C is a cool cupboard, not a fridge.

B.q: During a busy week you notice a critical item is running low. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait until it runs out, then order
Borrow some from the practice nearby
Order more and tell whoever manages stock
Ration it between surgeries until it runs out
B.why: Ordering at the reorder level and telling the stock manager keeps the item available and the records accurate.

whyNot.0: Waiting until it runs out could mean cancelled treatment.
whyNot.1: Borrowing doesn't solve the stock problem or update the records.
whyNot.3: Rationing risks running out and doesn't address the low stock.

B.q: Which pair of substances must be stored apart because they release a toxic gas if mixed?
options: Sodium hypochlorite and acids
Alginate powder and gypsum
Composite and bonding agent
Saline and chlorhexidine gluconate
B.why: Hypochlorite and acids react to release chlorine gas, so they are stored and used separately.

whyNot.1: Alginate and gypsum are routinely used together to make models.
whyNot.2: Composite and bonding agents are stored and used together safely.
whyNot.3: Saline and chlorhexidine don't react to form a toxic gas.

C.q: Why should you check the expiry date on a sterile single-use item before using it?
options: Sterility is only guaranteed up to that date
Out-of-date items cost the practice more money
The date shows when the item was manufactured
Expired items must be sterilised again before use
C.why: The manufacturer only guarantees sterility and performance up to the expiry date.

whyNot.1: Cost isn't the safety issue; patient safety is.
whyNot.2: The expiry date isn't the manufacture date.
whyNot.3: Single-use items must never be reprocessed; expired ones are discarded.

C.q: The morning fridge check shows a maximum reading of 12 °C overnight. What should you do first?
options: Reset the thermometer and carry on
Turn the thermostat colder and use the stock
Quarantine the contents and report it
Move everything into the staff fridge
C.why: Stock that has gone out of range may no longer be effective, so it is labelled 'do not use' and reported, and advice is sought before use.

whyNot.0: Resetting hides the problem and the stock may be ineffective.
whyNot.1: Turning it colder doesn't make stock that has overheated safe to use.
whyNot.3: A staff fridge isn't monitored or suitable for medicines.

C.q: Under COSHH, how should a hazardous chemical be stored?
options: Decanted into smaller unlabelled bottles
On the highest shelf, well out of the way
Next to the sink so spills can be rinsed
In its original container, labelled, lid on
C.why: Original labelled containers keep the hazard information and instructions with the chemical and prevent mix-ups.

whyNot.0: Unlabelled bottles hide the hazard and invite mistakes.
whyNot.1: Hazardous liquids should be stored low, not high, to reduce spill and splash risk.
whyNot.2: Next to a sink isn't a safe or secure storage place.

reteach.title: Think of a supermarket and your fridge at home
reteach.question: How does a supermarket make sure the milk at the front is the oldest, and what would you do if your fridge broke overnight?

blocks.body: Supermarket staff put fresh milk at the back so the older cartons get bought first. That's stock rotation. They know when to reorder before the shelf is empty, and they don't over-order or it goes off. If your fridge broke overnight you wouldn't trust the chicken in it just because it looked fine. The practice treats its stock the same way: oldest first, reorder before running out, and anything that's been kept at the wrong temperature is set aside until someone qualified says it's safe.

explain.body: Check every delivery against the order and delivery note, look for damage and expiry dates, put fridge items away first, and have POMs checked and locked away by an authorised person. Then update the stock records.

test.q: A delivery includes items that need refrigerating. When should they go into the fridge?
options: At the end of the day
After the stock records have all been updated
As soon as they have been checked in
When the next stock-take is done
test.why: Temperature-sensitive items go into the fridge straight after checking so they don't spend time out of range.

whyNot.0: Hours at room temperature could spoil them.
whyNot.1: Paperwork can wait; the fridge items can't.
whyNot.3: Stock-takes are periodic and far too late.

explain.body: First in, first out: new stock goes behind old so the earliest expiry is used first. Reorder at the minimum level, don't exceed the maximum, and tell the stock manager when a critical item runs low. Expired medicines go in the blue-lidded medicinal waste bin.

test.q: There are three boxes of the same bonding agent on the shelf, each with a different expiry date. Which should be used first?
options: The most recent delivery
The one that expires soonest
The box with the most left in it
The box that is already open
test.why: First in, first out: the stock that expires soonest is used first, which is why new deliveries go behind it.

whyNot.0: Using the newest first leaves older stock to expire.
whyNot.2: How much is left has nothing to do with which expires first.
whyNot.3: Being open doesn't mean it expires first; check the dates (and any opened-use limit).

explain.body: Keep it at 2–8 °C, for medicines only. Record current, minimum and maximum temperatures every working day and reset the thermometer. If it goes out of range, quarantine, report, record and seek advice. Glucagon kept out of the fridge (below 25 °C) has its shelf life cut to 18 months.

test.q: Which item is commonly kept in the dental practice medicines fridge?
options: Spare oxygen cylinder
Salbutamol inhaler
Glucagon injection kit
Dispersible aspirin tablets
test.why: Glucagon for hypoglycaemia is usually stored at 2–8 °C, or out of the fridge with a shortened expiry date.

whyNot.0: Oxygen cylinders are stored upright and secured, away from heat, not in a fridge.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol inhalers are kept at room temperature.
whyNot.3: Aspirin tablets are kept at room temperature.

explain.body: Every hazardous substance needs a risk assessment and a safety data sheet. Keep chemicals in original labelled containers with lids on, keep incompatibles (like hypochlorite and acids) apart, store flammables away from heat, keep corrosives low, and have spill kits ready.

test.q: Which document gives the hazards, safe storage and first aid for a chemical?
options: The supplier's delivery note
The stock record
The lab ticket
The safety data sheet
test.why: The safety data sheet (SDS) from the supplier sets out hazards, handling, storage, spillage and first aid, and informs the COSHH risk assessment.

whyNot.0: The delivery note lists what was delivered.
whyNot.1: The stock record tracks quantities and orders.
whyNot.2: A lab ticket is the dentist's prescription to the dental laboratory.
